116.0.s.en: (1) A request for deliverance from affliction

116.0.0.en: "I love the LORD, because he hath heard my voice and my supplications. Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, therefore will I call upon him as long as I live."

116.0.2.en: 1- When the writer of the psalm experienced God's concern to hear his prayers and supplications, he loved Him and loved prayer, so he continued to pray all day and every day, enjoying fellowship with God.

116.0.3.en: 2- God is a tender Father, therefore He inclined His ear to hear my prayer, and this is also humility on God's part, and great concern, especially since I am a sinner and a weak man and am ashamed to raise my voice, yet even so He loves me and comes down to me to hear me. This is a clear reference to the Incarnation of Christ, who came down to us from heaven to redeem us because He loves us so much; and so it becomes natural for us to love Him with all our heart.

116.0.4.en: 3- Prayer and calling upon God "as long as I live" does not mean only continuing in prayer throughout life on earth, but also continuing in prayer in the Kingdom forever.

116.1.0.en: "and the pains of hell gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow."

116.1.1.en: Compassed me: surrounded me and clung to me.

116.1.3.en: 1- The prophet David faced severe afflictions in his flight from the pursuit of his enemies, and was exposed to death many times. And he says "the cords of death," because cords are used in dividing land, as if his portion were death, and it surrounded him to the point of clinging to him, so he was in great sorrow and distress.

116.1.4.en: 2- The wars of the devil can be severe, surrounding the children of God and trying to make them fall into sin. And in their striving against them they bear much suffering and hardship, but it is precious in the sight of God.

116.2.0.en: "Then called I upon the name of the LORD; O LORD, I beseech thee, deliver my soul."

116.2.1.en: 1- The severity of the affliction drove the prophet David to call upon God. And "O" means taking refuge in God and entreating Him, for he has no deliverer in his affliction except God, and this comforted his heart and gave him rest.

116.2.2.en: 2- When David called upon the Lord in his affliction, and the effects of this prayer appeared on him in his calm and peace, this was a silent proclamation to those around him, that they might follow his example in their afflictions and seek God the deliverer from distresses.

116.2.3.en: God is very near to you, and He loves you, so do not be troubled if afflictions draw near to you, and even cling to you. For God is nearer to you than they are, and He is able to deliver you from them, so that you come out safe, and even benefit from the trial and grow strong spiritually.

116.3.0.en: "Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; yea, our God is merciful."

116.3.2.en: 1- God is gracious to His children, for He feels their weakness as human beings, and helps them to live with Him. But at the same time He is just, so He holds them to account for their sins, and we must therefore keep in mind His justice and enjoy His graciousness which encourages us. God declared Himself to Moses in this sense in one of his meetings with Him (Ex 34:6).

116.3.3.en: 2- He returns to affirm that God is merciful; for man has many sins, but God's mercy is wide, and by this He encourages him to repent, and whoever repents enjoys God's graciousness and mercy.

116.4.0.en: "The LORD preserveth the simple: I was brought low, and he helped me."

116.4.1.en: By the simple are meant little children, as in the Septuagint translation, for God preserves His children who feel their need of Him like children. David knew the way to God when he was brought low, that is, humbled himself, and became like children, as Christ asked in the New Testament (Mt 18:3), and He delivered him from all his afflictions.

116.5.0.en: "Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee."

116.5.1.en: 1- David expresses his joy, and asks his soul to return to her rest, because the Lord dealt bountifully with him when He delivered him from his enemies, and delivered him also from all turmoil and distress of soul, so he regained his peace. For the natural state of the spiritual man is to live in peace, and any turmoil is foreign to him, and if he takes refuge in God through prayer and spiritual striving, God gives him His rest.

116.5.2.en: 2- The rest mentioned points to the eternal rest, which is the greatest divine benefit that God gives to His children who believe in Him, who sought Him in humility and not out of any merit of their own; therefore this psalm is read in the funeral prayers, to recall the eternal rest into which the departed, over whose body the prayer is made, has entered.

116.6.0.en: "For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, and my feet from falling."

116.6.1.en: 1- David makes clear the reason for the rest which he received from God, which is:

116.6.2.en: a - That He delivered his soul from death as a result of his enemies' pursuit of him.

116.6.3.en: b - He dried his tears and comforted his sorrowful heart by lifting the affliction from him.

116.6.4.en: c - He kept his feet from slipping into various sins, such as taking vengeance on Saul, or any other sins. So God's protection was both material and spiritual.

116.6.5.en: 2- This verse applies to the person who has died, over whom we pray at the funeral, that God has delivered him from eternal death, and from the tears of anguish in Hades, and also from slipping into the desires that lead him to perdition.

116.6.6.en: 3- This verse is fitting for everyone who passes through afflictions and thanks God who keeps him during them.

116.7.0.en: "I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living."

116.7.1.en: 1- Verses (8, 9) were mentioned in Psalm 56:13. And the verse here means that since God has delivered me and kept me in all that went before, I must walk before Him in the land in which we live, that is, throughout our lives. Walking before God means pleasing Him with a pure life and keeping away from sin, in preparation for eternity, in which are the new earth and the new life.

116.7.2.en: 2- The repentant man who takes refuge in God in humility thanks God who delivered him, and returns to life with Him, and promises Him that he will walk in the fear and love of God, and please Him all the days of his life.

116.7.3.en: Life is an opportunity for repentance, so hasten to return to God if you fall, and be sure of His love; for He welcomes you and supports you to live with Him, and indeed you will make up for all that you have missed with a pure life that pleases Him, and so enjoy fellowship with Him.

116.8.s.en: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

116.8.0.en: "I believed, therefore have I spoken: I was greatly afflicted: I said in my haste, All men are liars."

116.8.1.en: 1- I believed that I would please God and walk before Him as in (v. 9). And this faith must be a practical faith, not only theoretical, and humility before God results from this faith, especially since the afflictions through which David passed brought him low, so he humbled himself before God that He might have mercy on him and deliver him.

116.8.2.en: 2- David felt that all men are liars, that is, vain, of no use, indeed that the whole world does not support him, and he too is vain and cannot support himself, and the only solution is faith in God and humility before Him.

116.9.0.en: "What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me? I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the LORD."

116.9.1.en: 1- The prophet David marvels at the multitude of God's benefits to him, so that he finds himself unable to repay God what is due, or to respond to Him and answer Him, for whatever David offers, the love of God is nothing before His many benefits. And he does not give God love as a favor from himself, but he only answers and responds to the divine love with which God began toward him.

116.9.2.en: 2- David feels that the least response to God is to share in His worship, and to drink the cups which were appointed at the feast of the Passover, which were cups of wine, a sign of joy, in addition to prayer, whether by reciting the psalms or any prayers.

116.9.3.en: 3- The cup of salvation which he takes is a clear symbol of the sacrifice of the New Testament, and of partaking of the Blood of Christ, in addition to His Body, and all this is accompanied by the prayers of the Liturgy, which are full of thanksgiving to God.

116.10.0.en: "I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people."

116.10.1.en: 1- If God has fulfilled His covenants and delivered me from my enemies and from every affliction, I must respond to Him and fulfill my vows which I promised Him during my affliction, as an expression of thanks and love to Him.

116.10.2.en: 2- These vows include prayers and the offering of sacrifices to God, and sharing the needy in eating of them, so they become love and thanks to God, and also love for others. And all this is done before the people of God, not for boasting, but to spread the spirit of thanksgiving among the people and to confirm the response to the divine love, and the necessity of fulfilling vows. All this used to happen in the Old Testament, and it can also happen in the New Testament, according to the kind of vow and what my lips have uttered, which must be fulfilled.

116.11.0.en: "Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints."

116.11.1.en: 1- He who reveres God and fears Him, so that he cares for His worship, drinks the cup of joy, calls upon the name of the Lord and pays his vows, this man, if he dies, his death is precious and honorable in the sight of the Lord, and He prepares for him a place of rest and joy in heaven.

116.11.2.en: 2- By the saints is meant Christ, the martyrs, and all who die in the service of the Lord, such as the Apostles, the priests, and everyone who serves the Lord. The death of Christ was precious in the sight of the Father, because by it the redemption of humanity was accomplished. And the death of the martyrs, and of all who fall asleep in the Lord, is precious in His sight, and He gives them rest from the labors of earth and rewards them with the glories of heaven.

116.11.3.en: 3- If Christ died for me and offered me the cup of salvation, which is His Blood on the altar of the New Testament, it is natural for me to respond to His love and die to sin that I may live for Him, and when I die in the body, this will be precious in His sight.

116.12.0.en: "O LORD, truly I am thy servant; I am thy servant, and the son of thine handmaid: thou hast loosed my bonds."

116.12.2.en: 1- The prophet David declares his submission to God and his faith in Him, saying "I am thy servant" and also "the son of thine handmaid," from which it is understood that David's mother was a pious woman who brought him up with a spiritual upbringing. So because of his faith and the faith of his mother, God blessed him and loosed his bonds, that is, brought him out of his afflictions.

116.12.3.en: 2- This verse applies to Christ, who was in the flesh in the form of a servant, and is the son of the handmaid of the Lord, the Virgin Mary, who declared this to the angel who brought her the good tidings (Lk 1:38); and for this reason the Father loosed His bonds by His resurrection from the dead.

116.13.0.en: "I will offer to thee the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and will call upon the name of the LORD. I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people, In the courts of the LORD's house, in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem. Praise ye the LORD."

116.13.1.en: The verses mentioned before in (vv. 13, 14) are repeated here to affirm his longing to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving to God accompanied by prayers, with the fulfilling of vows before all the people, and in front of the house of the Lord. And the sacrifices are not limited to animal sacrifices, which are thanksgiving to God, but also include sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving. The meaning of this is that David was far from Jerusalem, but his heart was attached to God and to worship before His house.

116.13.2.en: May you take care to thank God for His works with you, especially after afflictions. Do not be content with asking for your needs, or for deliverance from the affliction, but also thank Him, to prove your love for God and to increase your sense of His love.

116.13.3.en: A call to all to praise God "O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people" (v. 1) Introduction:

116.13.4.en: 1- Its author: the psalm has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms whose author is unknown. There is an opinion that its author is the prophet David.

116.13.5.en: 2- When was it written? There are two opinions:

116.13.6.en: a - It was written in the days of David when the Jewish nation was in its strength and extent, so David calls the whole world to believe in God and praise Him.

116.13.7.en: b - It was written after the captivity, at the return of the people to Jerusalem, with its writer longing that the nations among whom he had lived would believe and praise God.

116.13.8.en: 3- This psalm calls the whole world to praise God for His many mercies, His faithfulness, and His care for men. It encourages every believer to praise, and to encourage those around him to do so.

116.13.9.en: 4- It is a Messianic psalm which speaks of the Church of the New Testament, which includes all nations and peoples.

116.13.10.en: 5- Christ referred to this psalm after His resurrection, when He called His disciples to preach and to make disciples of all nations (Mt 28:18-20; Mk 16:15-16).

116.13.11.en: 6- The Apostle Paul quoted from this psalm in his epistle to the Romans (Rom 15:11).

116.13.12.en: 7- This psalm is fitting for every believer when he begins his day, so that he repeats this psalm to encourage himself and those around him to praise God, as Pope Kyrillos VI used to do.

116.13.13.en: 8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya at the beginning of the prayer of Vespers, because the salvation of Christ included not only the Jews but also the Gentiles, who are symbolized by those of the eleventh hour, that is, the hour of sunset, whom Christ received and gave them salvation and a place in His Kingdom.

117.0.s.en: (3) Thanks to God who does good to me

117.0.0.en: "O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people."

117.0.1.en: 1- This verse represents the longings of the prophet David, and of all the pious in the Old Testament, who wished that all nations and peoples would believe, and praise God and thank Him.

117.0.2.en: 2- It is a clear prophecy of the Church of the New Testament, which includes all nations and peoples, many of whom believe and praise God in His churches.

117.0.3.en: 3- The praise is completed by all peoples in heaven, where there is neither Jew nor Gentile, but all believe in Christ and praise Him forever.

117.1.0.en: "For his merciful kindness is great toward us: and the truth of the LORD endureth for ever. Praise ye the LORD."

117.1.1.en: 1- God's mighty mercy appeared in offering salvation to the whole world, which had been hinted at in the Old Testament by the acceptance of a few of the Gentiles into the faith, who even came to be in the lineage of Christ, such as Rahab the harlot and Ruth the Gentile. But it became perfectly clear in the salvation offered on the cross, which the Apostles proclaimed in the whole world, and many believed and praised God.

117.1.2.en: 2- God's faithfulness appeared in His fulfilling His promises, for He promised Eve that her seed would crush the head of the serpent, and her seed is Christ who bound Satan on the cross. And all His promises which the prophets uttered were fulfilled in the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption of the whole world, and the acceptance of faith by the Gentiles.

117.1.3.en: May you pray for all those around you, that they may share with you your love for God and praise Him with faith and joy, so that you rejoice and gladden the heart of God, and He works in the hearts of many.

117.1.4.en: Rejoicing in the blessings of salvation "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: because his mercy endureth for ever" (v. 1) Introduction:

117.1.5.en: 1- Its author: there are two opinions:

117.1.6.en: a - The prophet David, for he expresses his attachment to the worship of the Lord in His house, and the power of God which supported him against his enemies.

117.1.7.en: b - An unknown writer who wrote it after the return from the captivity; because the psalm has no title, that is, it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is unknown.

117.1.8.en: 2- When was it written? There are two possibilities:

117.1.9.en: a - Toward the end of David's life, after the moving of the ark of the covenant of God and his victories over his surrounding enemies.

117.1.10.en: b - After the return from the captivity and the rebuilding of the house of the Lord.

117.1.11.en: 3- This psalm expresses the salvation of the Lord however severe the afflictions, so it is fitting for every believer who is exposed to afflictions, so that he prays it to be strengthened and to make his faith firm.

117.1.12.en: 4- It is the last of the Egyptian Hallel psalms (Ps 113-118), which the Jews chant after eating the Passover, rejoicing in the salvation of the Lord.

117.1.13.en: 5- This psalm is the prayer of Christ with His disciples after eating the Passover (Mt 26:30).

117.1.14.en: 6- This psalm is prayed at the feast of Tabernacles, since it mentions in (v. 24) that this is the day which the Lord has made. And because of the importance of the feast of Tabernacles, it used to be called the feast, or the day, and it is understood to be the feast of Tabernacles (Neh 8:14; Ps 81:3). And the refrain that was repeated at the feast of Tabernacles is (v. 26), and the palm branch that was used at the feast of Tabernacles they call "Hosanna." In addition, at the feast of Tabernacles the rite of the lights was very important, as (v. 27) mentions. And this psalm was prayed each day of the six days of the celebration of the feast of Tabernacles, and prayed seven times on the seventh day of the feast.

117.1.15.en: 7- This psalm is a liturgical psalm, for we understand that it was chanted at the feast of the Passover and the feast of Tabernacles, and the king, the priest and the people shared in chanting it. Each group chants a part of it, and the other group responds. And when Christ chanted it after the Passover, He would say a part of it and the disciples would respond.

117.1.16.en: 8- This psalm is one of the strong Messianic psalms, because it speaks of Christ, who is the Righteous One who bore many afflictions and lived in righteousness, and He is the chief cornerstone.

117.1.17.en: 9- This psalm is used in the rite of the Church, as a part of it is chanted every Sunday at the offering of the Lamb (v. 24), and it is said in the psalm of the feast of the Resurrection (vv. 24-26). And it is prayed on the second day of the feast of the Cross (vv. 15, 16, 28).

117.1.18.en: 10- The New Testament quoted much from this psalm: the Jews chanted (vv. 25, 26) when they welcomed Christ as He entered Jerusalem (Mt 21:9). And Christ quoted from it (vv. 22, 23) in His dialogue with the Jews (Mt 21:42). In addition to the quotation by the Apostle Paul (Heb 13:

117.1.19.en: 6) and Peter quoted from it in (Acts 4:11; 1 Pet 2:7).

117.1.20.en: 11- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Vespers, in which they took down the body of Christ from the cross, so we remember the sufferings of Christ which He completed for us, to grant us salvation, as this psalm makes clear.
